subject: Renal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has involuntary leakage of urine when she sneezes, laughs, or lifts heavy objects. She has a history of two vaginal deliveries and obesity. A bladder stress test directly demonstrates leakage from the urethra with coughing.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Urgency incontinence due to detrusor overactivity
Overflow incontinence due to urinary retention
Mixed incontinence with both stress and urgency features
Functional incontinence from impaired mobility
Stress incontinence due to outlet incompetence with increased intra-abdominal pressure

explanation_correct: Stress incontinence results from outlet incompetence (urethral hypermobility or intrinsic sphincter deficiency) and produces leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure such as sneezing or lifting; the bladder stress test is positive. Associations include obesity, pregnancy, vaginal delivery, and prostate surgery. Treatment includes pelvic floor muscle (Kegel) exercises, weight loss, and pessaries.

explanation_incorrect.A: Urgency incontinence leaks with an immediate urge to void due to detrusor overactivity, not with raised intra-abdominal pressure.
explanation_incorrect.B: Overflow incontinence involves incomplete emptying, overfilling, and an increased postvoid residual rather than exertional leakage.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mixed incontinence has both stress and urgency features; this patient describes only leakage with increased abdominal pressure.
explanation_incorrect.D: Functional incontinence results from inability to reach a toilet (eg, impaired mobility), not from outlet incompetence with a positive stress test.

educationalObjective: Stress incontinence leaks with increased intra-abdominal pressure from outlet incompetence; Kegel exercises, weight loss, and pessaries are treatments.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has sudden, strong urges to void followed immediately by involuntary leakage. She recently had a urinary tract infection. There is no leakage with coughing or exercise.
question: Which of the following best identifies the type of incontinence and a typical treatment?

options.text: Stress incontinence; treated with pessaries
Overflow incontinence; treated with catheterization
Mixed incontinence; treated with weight loss alone
Urgency incontinence due to detrusor overactivity; treated with bladder training and antimuscarinics
Stress incontinence due to intrinsic sphincter deficiency; treated with Kegel exercises

explanation_correct: Urgency incontinence results from detrusor overactivity and causes leakage with the urge to void immediately. It is associated with bladder irritation from UTI, stones, tumors, or pelvic radiation. Treatment includes pelvic floor physical therapy, bladder training (timed voiding, distraction or relaxation techniques), antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin for overactive bladder, and mirabegron/vibegron.

explanation_incorrect.A: Stress incontinence leaks with increased intra-abdominal pressure rather than with a strong urge; pessaries are used for stress, not urgency, incontinence.
explanation_incorrect.B: Overflow incontinence results from incomplete emptying with a high postvoid residual and is managed with catheterization and relief of obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mixed incontinence requires both stress and urgency features; this patient has urgency symptoms without exertional leakage.
explanation_incorrect.E: Intrinsic sphincter deficiency causes stress incontinence, not leakage immediately following an urge to void.

educationalObjective: Urgency incontinence is detrusor overactivity with leakage right after the urge; treat with bladder training, antimuscarinics (oxybutynin), or mirabegron.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 72-year-old man with BPH reports urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and continuous dribbling. Ultrasound shows a markedly elevated postvoid residual volume. He also has diabetes with polyuria.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's incontinence?

options.text: Detrusor overactivity with leakage at the time of a strong urge
Incomplete emptying from outlet obstruction (BPH) causing overflow with an increased postvoid residual
Urethral hypermobility causing leakage with Valsalva
Bladder irritation from a urinary tract infection
A combination of stress and urgency incontinence only

explanation_correct: Overflow incontinence results from incomplete emptying due to detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction, producing leakage with overfilling and an increased postvoid residual on catheterization or ultrasound. Associations include urinary retention, polyuria (eg, diabetes), bladder outlet obstruction (eg, BPH), and spinal cord injury. Treatment includes catheterization and relieving the obstruction (eg, alpha-blockers for BPH).

explanation_incorrect.A: Detrusor overactivity produces urgency incontinence with leakage at the time of an urge, not dribbling from overfilling with a high postvoid residual.
explanation_incorrect.C: Urethral hypermobility is a cause of stress incontinence with leakage on Valsalva or coughing, which is not the mechanism here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bladder irritation from UTI causes urgency incontinence, not chronic urinary retention with a markedly elevated postvoid residual.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mixed incontinence combines stress and urgency features, not the overflow due to outlet obstruction described in this patient.

educationalObjective: Overflow incontinence is incomplete emptying with high postvoid residual from outlet obstruction (BPH) or detrusor underactivity; treat with catheterization and alpha-blockers.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 50-year-old woman reports two distinct patterns: leakage when she lifts her toddler with no warning, and sudden leakage right after feeling a strong urge to void, which she attributes to recurrent UTIs.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate classification and management plan?

options.text: Pure stress incontinence; pelvic floor exercises and pessaries only
Pure urgency incontinence; antimuscarinics and bladder training only
Mixed incontinence with both stress and urgency features; address both with pelvic floor therapy/bladder training and consider antimuscarinics
Overflow incontinence; catheterization and relief of obstruction
Functional incontinence; environmental modifications only

explanation_correct: Mixed incontinence has features of both stress and urgency incontinence, as this patient demonstrates with leakage both on exertion and with urgency. Management should target both components: pelvic floor muscle strengthening and bladder training, with antimuscarinics (eg, oxybutynin) or mirabegron for the urge component. Treating only one component would leave the other symptoms unaddressed.

explanation_incorrect.A: Managing only the stress component with pelvic floor exercises and pessaries would ignore her prominent urgency symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.B: Treating only urgency with antimuscarinics and bladder training would leave the exertional (stress) leakage untreated.
explanation_incorrect.D: There is no evidence of incomplete emptying, urinary retention, or an elevated postvoid residual to suggest overflow incontinence.
explanation_incorrect.E: Functional incontinence relates to inability to reach a toilet, not to the combined stress and urgency symptoms described here.

educationalObjective: Mixed incontinence combines stress and urgency features; management must address both components.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 68-year-old man has bothersome urinary hesitancy, a weak stream, and dribbling due to BPH. Postvoid residual is elevated, and he has overflow incontinence.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Catheterization and relief of obstruction, for example with alpha-blockers for BPH
Antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin to reduce detrusor overactivity
Kegel exercises and pessaries to improve outlet competence
Bladder training with timed voiding and distraction techniques
Mirabegron to relax the detrusor muscle

explanation_correct: Overflow incontinence is due to incomplete emptying from outlet obstruction (such as BPH) or detrusor underactivity. Management is catheterization and relief of the obstruction; alpha-blockers relax smooth muscle at the bladder neck and prostate in BPH. Antimuscarinics and mirabegron are used for urgency incontinence from detrusor overactivity, and Kegel exercises/pessaries are for stress incontinence.

explanation_incorrect.B: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic used for urgency incontinence and can worsen urinary retention in a patient with outlet obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Kegel exercises and pessaries are treatments for stress incontinence from outlet incompetence, not for overflow from obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bladder training with timed voiding is a behavioral therapy for urgency incontinence, not for relieving mechanical obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist used for overactive bladder (urgency incontinence), not for overflow incontinence due to BPH.

educationalObjective: Overflow incontinence from BPH is managed by catheterization and relieving obstruction with alpha-blockers, not by antimuscarinics or pelvic floor therapy.
